name: Large merchant sailing ships
note: Rome already operates grain ships of 350 tonnes or more to Alexandria; the Fayum papyri and wrecks confirm sophisticated hull design and large crews.

name: Mortise-and-tenon hull construction
note: Rome's Mediterranean shipwrights already lock planks edge-to-edge with interlocking joints; this is shell-first construction, building the hull shell before framing.

name: Square sail with brails
note: The square sail hangs from a yard; brails (lines running to the yard) gather it up when not needed; it cannot work to windward.

name: Spritsail
note: A sail rigged diagonally across the mast with a spar (the sprit); gives some directional control compared to pure square rig.

name: Lead sheathing against shipworm
note: Lead sheet nailed over the underwater hull prevents shipworm (Teredo) boring into timber; Rome has done this for decades; it is perishable and must be renewed regularly.

name: Steering oars
note: Large oars mounted on each quarter (side) of the stern, worked by pilots; slow and inefficient on large hulls with a following sea.

name: Anchor
note: Heavy iron-shank anchor with wooden flukes; holds a ship in sand or mud; chains and cable are rope, which cost money to replace.

name: Sounding lines
note: A knotted rope with a lead weight; tossed overboard to measure water depth and bottom type; pilots memorize landmarks and feel the bottom.

name: Coastal pilotage
note: Experienced pilots guide ships via visual landmarks, tides, and memory; safe within sight of land; at sea they are lost.

name: Pharos lighthouse
note: The great tower at Alexandria with fire beacon at night; one of Rome's most famous navigational aids; visible for miles at sea.

name: Artificial harbours in hydraulic concrete
note: Rome builds harbours at Portus and Caesarea using pozzolanic concrete that sets underwater; breakwaters and jetties protect anchorages.

name: Monsoon route to India
note: The Red Sea and Indian Ocean route is now known to sail southwest with summer monsoon to India, return northeast with winter monsoon; still hazardous and slow.

name: Sternpost rudder
note: A single flat board hung vertically at the stern from iron pintles, turned by a tiller; much more responsive than steering oars on large hulls, especially in following seas.

name: Lateen sail
note: A triangular sail rigged along the mast at an angle, known in the Mediterranean; can sail 6 to 8 points from the wind, not 11-12 like modern fore-and-aft, but a real improvement over square.

name: Fore-and-aft rig
note: Sails set along the length of the mast rather than across it; requires stronger masts and better carpentry; allows true beating to windward with multiple tacks.

name: Bowsprit
note: A spar extending forward from the bow to which jibs are attached; spreads the sail plan and improves balance; very exposed to breaking in heavy seas.

name: Jib sail
note: Triangular sail forward of the mast; helps turn the ship and improves windward work; adds to total canvas with minimal weight.

name: Multiple masts
note: Ships with two or three masts can carry more sail, balance trim better, and sacrifice fewer sails if one mast is damaged; requires significantly stronger hulls.

name: Carvel planking
note: Planks laid edge-to-edge and edge-fitted flush; smoother and stronger than clinker, allows larger ships; requires excellent carpentry and precise tools.

name: Clinker planking
note: Planks overlap like roof shingles and are rivetted at the overlap; easier to build than carvel, lighter, more flexible; popular in northern Europe.

name: Skeleton-first hull construction
note: Build the frame (ribs) first, then plank over it, not vice versa; cheaper and faster, scales to much larger ships, and uses timber more efficiently; requires a fundamental rethinking of carpentry.

name: Lodestone knowledge
note: Rome knows that lodestones attract iron; the knowledge that this is true even when spinning, and points north, is not yet recorded in the literature.

name: Dry compass card
note: A card with 32 points marked, pivoted on a needle magnetized by rubbing with lodestone, enclosed in a box; far more stable than a wet compass floating in oil.

name: Log line for speed
note: A light wooden board (the log) on a long knotted line; thrown overboard, it stays in place while the ship moves; count the knots paid out in a sand-glass interval to find speed.

name: Traverse board
note: A board with holes and a peg; log the ship's course and speed every hour; sum them at the end of the watch to estimate position; crude but systematic.

name: Cross-staff for latitude
note: Hold a calibrated wooden cross at arm's length; move the cross-bar until it aligns the sun with the horizon; read the angle; gives latitude to within a degree or so.

name: Backstaff for latitude
note: Observe the sun's shadow rather than looking at it; more accurate than the cross-staff; still limited by eye and wind movement; typically accurate to 0.3 degrees.

name: Sextant for latitude and more
note: Uses mirrors and a vernier scale; measure angles up to 120 degrees; accurate to 0.1 degree; also measures stellar altitudes for latitude at night; the standard instrument for three centuries.

name: Magnetic compass
note: A pivoted compass card with a magnetized needle shows north in any weather, by day or night, independent of landmarks; one of the pivotal inventions for open-sea navigation.

name: Navigation charts
note: Systematically plot known coastlines, harbours, and hazards; use magnetic compass rose; accumulate centuries of observation; early charts are crude but better than guesswork.

name: Mercator projection
note: Project the globe onto a cylinder; latitude and longitude become straight lines; a rhumb line (constant compass heading) becomes straight; game-changing for charts.

name: Lead-line and hydrographic survey
note: Systematically map harbour depths and holding ground; use a marked line with lead weight and hollow underside (carries samples of sand, shells, mud); plot on charts.

name: Drydock
note: An enclosed basin with gates; flood to float the ship in, then pump or drain to expose the hull for repairs and careening; very expensive, worth it only for major harbours.

name: Marine chronometer
note: A clock that keeps time to better than 1 second per day at sea despite temperature swings and ship motion; solved by Harrison via bimetallic compensation and friction balance; the breakthrough for longitude.

name: Lunar distance method for longitude
note: Measure the angle between the moon and a known star; look up the time of that angle in pre-computed tables; convert time to longitude; works without a chronometer but requires superlative tables and a calm hand.

name: Copper-sheathed hull
note: Thin copper sheet nailed over the hull below the waterline; resists shipworm better than lead and does not pit; very expensive but saves years of ship life.

name: Paddle wheel
note: Large wheels with flat paddles on each side, driven by a steam engine; inherently inefficient (submerges too much water near the surface) and loses power in a heavy sea.

name: Screw propeller
note: A helical blade (like an Archimedean screw) beneath the stern, spinning at high speed; far more efficient than a paddle wheel, especially in heavy seas and at full speed.

name: Iron hull
note: A ship built entirely of iron plates riveted together; floats because the average density is low (air inside); immune to shipworm and rot; three times the tonnage of wood for the same structural weight.

name: Compartmented hull
note: Watertight bulkheads divide the hull into sections; if one section is breached, it floods but does not sink the ship; saves more lives than lifeboats.

name: Steel hull
note: Steel is stronger and tougher than iron; allows thinner, lighter hulls for the same strength; standard by 1890; vastly better fatigue resistance than iron.

name: Compound and triple expansion engine
note: Multiple cylinders at different pressures; steam expands through each in turn; triples fuel efficiency compared to a simple engine; coal consumption becomes the limiting factor.

name: Steam turbine at sea
note: Steam jets hit curved blades on a fast-spinning rotor; much smaller, lighter, and cheaper than reciprocating engines for the same power; direct drive to a propeller.

name: Diesel engine ship
note: Internal combustion engine burning fuel oil; more efficient than steam turbines and no need to carry water or boilers; standard in merchant ships by 1920.

name: Torpedo
note: A self-propelled warhead driven by a small steam engine or compressed air, launched from a tube; detonates on contact or by timed fuse; extends the range of naval combat beyond line of sight.

name: Submarine
note: A small strong hull that submerges; propelled by electric motors on batteries or a diesel on the surface; requires precise depth control, air supply, and crew training; first military use in WWI.

name: Submarine telegraph cable
note: Copper conductor insulated with gutta percha (unobtainable), wrapped in iron armor; gutta percha fails, so use bitumen and later synthetic rubber instead, accepting higher loss.

name: Sonar and echo sounding
note: Transmit an acoustic pulse into water, listen for the echo; measures depth and detects underwater objects; replaces the lead-line and adds a new dimension to navigation.

name: Lifeboat
note: A strong open boat carried on davits (cranes); can be launched quickly; holds a fraction of the crew; crew discipline and adequate numbers matter far more than equipment.

name: Lighthouse with Fresnel lens
note: A stepped glass lens focuses light from a lantern into a parallel beam visible for 20 miles; vastly brighter than a simple lens; standard by 1850.

name: Buoy
note: A floating marker anchored to a rock or sandbar; guides ships around hazards; a coded system of colors and shapes lets pilots recognize them at distance.

name: Canal lock
note: An enclosed chamber with gates; fill to float a boat up, drain to lower it down; allows ships to traverse rivers with different water levels and connects seas at different heights.

name: Dredging
note: Mechanically scoop mud and sediment from a harbour or river bottom; deepens channels and prevents silting; essential for maintaining harbours over decades.

name: Diving bell
note: An air-filled bell lowered to the seafloor on a rope; a diver climbs in, breathes the air, works for a few minutes, then is pulled up; depth limited to 40 feet and time to 15 minutes.

name: Diving suit and air pump
note: Waterproof suit with helmet, fed air by hose from a steam-driven pump on the surface; allows work at 200 feet for an hour; nitrogen narcosis and decompression sickness are poorly understood.

name: Astronomical tables
note: Pre-compute the position of the sun, moon, and stars for centuries ahead; used for latitude, longitude by lunar distances, and checking accuracy; the Nautical Almanac.

name: Water-tube boiler
note: Tubes carry hot combustion gases; water flows in separate tubes; higher heat transfer and safety; pressures to 300 psi and higher; faster steam production than fire-tube boilers.

name: Fuel oil burner
note: Atomize fuel oil and spray it into a furnace; burns cleaner and hotter than coal; enables diesel engines and high-pressure steam boilers; requires fuel oil supply infrastructure.

name: Electromagnetic wave theory
note: Maxwell showed that light is an electromagnetic wave; this understanding underpins sonar, radar, and radio; converts acoustic and optical problems into a unified framework.
